newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Grain - Prices rise on export deals.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Grain - Prices rise on export deals.

text.p: Australian domestic grain prices rose last week on the strength of significant well-priced export deals by the Australian Wheat Board (AWB).

Markets were betting by the close of last week that the AWB would increase its pool price estimates by at least A$5.00 a tonne to A$190.00 for benchmark grade Australian Standard White (ASW). The revision, scheduled for Monday afternoon, could raise prices by as much as A$10.00 a tonne, some traders said.
Grain cash prices rose by A$5.00 a tonne across-the-board last week, traders said on Friday.
The main influence was from export deals with Pakistan and Iran at prices of about A$200.00 a tonne, well up on the AWB pool price estimate of A$185.00 a tonne
The AWB announced during the week that it had sold 112,000 tonnes of ASW to Pakistan as part of that country's tender for 315,000 tonnes of white wheat for February delivery.
China-owned trading house CITIC Food Australia confirmed that it had negotiated 45,000 tonnes of the tender at US$156.285 a tonne, or almost exactly A$200.00 a tonne.
The AWB later announced it had sold 1.5 million tonnes of ASW to Iran, now Australia's biggest wheat customer.
Price was not disclosed but AWB chairman Trevor Flugge told Reuters price was about the same as in the Pakistan sale.
"Reports we're getting are that the AWB has been selling offshore at A$200.00 a tonne FOB," Bill Mitchell of New England Agricultural Traders told Reuters on Friday.
Some of that may be offset by the board not being able to take full advantage of the drop in Australian dollar, but there was still room for a A$5.00-A$10.00 pool price rise, he said.
Backed by a bumper good-quality crop and an aggressive marketing programme which does not involve price-cuts, the AWB said on Friday it was pleased with performance.
Shipping records were being broken, record tonnages were being sold for this stage of the marketing programme and more than 50 percent of projected exports had been sold, it said.
The A$5.00 a tonne rise in domestic grains cash prices, in a more interesting weeek for Australian grain markets, took sorghum up to A$147.00 and ASW to A$162.00, delivered Newcastle.
Sydney Futures Exchange wheat prices remained trapped by a lack of market liquidity, but showed signs of moving ahead as portents turned more bullish over the week.
On Friday, July 1997 and November 1997 rose by A$3.50 and A$6.50 a tonne respectively on modest volume, as interest switched to more distant contracts.

Over the week, futures settlement prices rose by about A$5.00 for most contracts, with January 1997 rising to A$165.50 from A$161.50, March to A$165.50 from A$157.50, September to A$158.00 from A$149.50 and May 1998 to A$153.50 from A$151.50.

Australia's 1996/97 wheat is almost all in, with only Western Australia continuing to harvest. NSW grain handling cooperative GrainCorp announced during the week that it had received 8.14 million tonnes of grain and that the 1983/84
record of 8.3 million tonnes was expected to be overtaken.

Trade belief strengthened over the week that Australia was headed for a 23-24 million tonne wheat crop, ahead of the record 22 million tonnes crop of 1983/84 and up on official estimates of about 21.5 million for the current season.
